entries.claim: Is it true that Manusmriti says bad things about women?
entries.scenarioShort: Doesn't Manusmriti treat women as inferior?
entries.quickAnswer: Yes, controversial verses exist. But we don't have the original Manusmriti, surviving manuscripts differ, and the same text tells families to honor women—saying a family prospers when its women are respected and happy.

points.title: YES, THOSE VERSES EXIST
points.text: Some versions of the Manusmriti we have today do contain verses about women that we'd consider unfair by today's standards. That's real — don't pretend otherwise.

points.title: BUT WE DON'T HAVE THE ORIGINAL
points.text: The text passed through many centuries of handwritten copies. More than fifty surviving manuscripts have been studied by scholars, and they don't all say exactly the same thing. This shows that the text changed during its long history of transmission, and scholars examine individual passages to determine whether some may be later additions.

points.title: HERE'S WHAT ELSE MANUSMRITI SAYS
points.text: The same text contains one of its most famous lines — and it says the opposite.
points.verse: Where women are honored, there the Devatās rejoice; where women are not honored, all sacred actions become fruitless.

points.title: SO WHY THE CONTRADICTION?
points.text: Nobody knows for certain. Ancient texts copied by hand over many centuries can pick up changes and additions along the way.

points.title: DID OUTSIDERS MAKE THIS WORSE?
points.text: During British rule, colonial administrators chose Manusmriti as an important source for creating what they called 'Hindu law.' This gave one Dharmaśāstra much more importance as a single law book than it had traditionally held across India. Some historians believe colonial interpretations also made Indian traditions appear more backward and divided — how much that affected this specific text is still debated, so it's worth knowing what the evidence establishes versus what remains an open question.

entries.say: Yes, those verses exist in versions we have today. But we don't have Manu's original, the manuscripts differ, and the same Manusmriti says families prosper where women are honored. So it's more complicated than one quotation.
entries.sources: Manusmriti 3.55–3.60; Patrick Olivelle's textual and critical scholarship on the Mānava-Dharmaśāstra; scholarship on the development of Anglo-Hindu law under British colonial administration.
entries.keywords: Manusmriti, women, yatra nāryastu pūjyante, manuscript transmission, Patrick Olivelle, colonial India, Hindu law, 3.56, honor women

entries.scenarioShort: Isn't Krishna kind of a player with like a thousand girlfriends?
entries.quickAnswer: No. Krishna did not have “1,000 girlfriends.” That claim mixes together different stories and gives them a modern meaning they did not have. The gopīs of Vṛndāvana are part of the sacred Rāsa Līlā, which the tradition understands as a story of extraordinary devotion to the Divine—not Krishna having hundreds or thousands of girlfriends.

points.title: THEN WHAT ABOUT “THOUSANDS OF WIVES”?
points.text: That's a different story from a different period of Krishna's life. It concerns thousands of captive women whom Krishna freed from Narakāsura. In the traditional understanding, Krishna's acceptance of these women protected their dignity and gave them social protection after their captivity—not a story about Krishna collecting thousands of girlfriends. So neither story supports the claim that “Krishna had 1,000 girlfriends.”

entries.say: No. That's not what the stories say. The gopīs are part of Rāsa Līlā, a sacred story about complete devotion to the Divine—not thousands of girlfriends. The separate story about thousands of women is about women Krishna freed from captivity and then protected, not a collection of girlfriends.
entries.sources: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29–33 (rāsa līlā); Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.59 (Narakāsura episode).
entries.keywords: Krishna, gopis, girlfriends, wives, raas leela, rasa lila, Vrindavan, Dwarka, Narakasura, bhakti, devotion

entries.claim: What is Rāsa Līlā? Was Krishna dancing with other people's wives?
entries.scenarioShort: Isn't the Rasa Lila just Krishna sneaking around with married women?
entries.quickAnswer: No. Rāsa Līlā is not presented in Sanātana tradition as Krishna “sneaking around with married women.” It is a sacred līlā about the gopīs' extraordinary bhakti—their complete, selfless love and devotion to Krishna as the Divine. The Bhāgavata itself warns that Krishna's actions here should never be imitated as ordinary human behavior.

points.title: WHAT IS RĀSA LĪLĀ REALLY ABOUT?
points.text: The gopīs' love for Krishna is understood in the bhakti tradition as prema—complete, selfless devotion to the Divine—not ordinary desire. During the Rāsa Līlā, Krishna appears beside each gopī individually. One meaning traditionally drawn from this is beautiful: the Divine can be completely present for every devotee at the same time.

points.title: THEN WHY DOES IT USE THE LANGUAGE OF LOVE?
points.text: Sanātana traditions use different human relationships to help us understand ways of loving the Divine—as a servant, friend, parent, or beloved. The gopīs express mādhurya bhakti: love of the Divine with complete intimacy and surrender. Human love provides the language, but the subject is the soul's love for the Divine.

points.title: DOES THE BHĀGAVATA ITSELF ADDRESS THIS QUESTION?
points.text: Yes—and this is important. Immediately after the Rāsa Līlā, the Bhāgavata warns that an ordinary person should never imitate Krishna's actions. Krishna is being presented as Īśvara, not as an ordinary human being whose behavior people should copy. So reading Rāsa Līlā as Krishna showing that it's okay to sneak around with married women is almost the opposite of what the text itself tells its reader to do.
points.verse: One who is not a great controller should never imitate the behavior of ruling personalities, even mentally.

entries.say: Rāsa Līlā isn't a story telling people to behave that way. It's a sacred līlā about complete devotion to Krishna as the Divine. In fact, the Bhāgavata itself warns ordinary people not to imitate Krishna's actions in this līlā.
entries.sources: Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29–33 (rāsa līlā); Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.30 (Śuka's warning against imitation, verified against Bhaktivedanta VedaBase Sanskrit edition); commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmī (14th–15th c.), Jīva Gosvāmī and Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura (16th–17th c.) on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. Traditional commentators have explained its devotional meaning for centuries.
entries.keywords: rasa lila, gopis, bhakti, prema, madhurya, devotion, married women, imitation, Vrindavan, Sridhara Swami, Jiva Goswami, Vishvanatha Chakravarti
